meta.title: Human Resources
meta.range: HSC topic · 25% of course time · the contribution of human resource management to business performance

boxes.label: Examinable
boxes.bodyHtml: Role of human resource management, key influences (stakeholders, legal, economic, technological, social, ethics/CSR), processes of HRM (acquisition, development, maintenance, separation), strategies in HRM (leadership style, job design, recruitment, training and development, performance management, rewards, global), workplace disputes and effectiveness of HRM — all Learn To and Learn About dot points.

boxes.label: Format reminder
boxes.bodyHtml: The HSC Business Studies exam draws on all four topics: Section I is 20 multiple-choice questions, Section II is short-answer questions spanning all topics, Section III is a business-report extended response, and Section IV offers a choice of extended-response questions by topic.

summary.note: Covers all six syllabus sub-topics: role, key influences, processes, strategies, workplace disputes and effectiveness of HRM.

groups.title: Role of human resource management
points: Human resource management (HRM) manages the relationship between employer and employee; businesses typically spend more than half their total costs on staff, so employees should be treated as an asset, not just an expense.

HR's four main functions: acquisition (attracting and hiring staff), development (improving skills and knowledge), maintenance (managing legal responsibilities and rewarding performance) and separation (employees leaving the business).

The strategic role of HR is to help the business maximise profit through productivity — maximised through open communication and goal setting, eliminating conflict, motivation (rewarding performance) and a positive work environment.

Interdependence: operations needs HR to hire and train staff who can operate machinery and manage quality (and to manage redundancies when operations outsources or automates); marketing needs HR to hire researchers, advertisers and salespeople with the right communication skills; finance needs HR to determine reward sizes and training budgets, while providing HR with the funds to do so.

Outsourcing HR functions (e.g. using a recruitment agency) can access specialised skills and lower costs, but risks employee unrest between in-house and outsourced staff and loss of control over how functions are performed.

Contractors differ from outsourcing in being engaged for a specific project rather than an ongoing function. Domestic contractors offer local market knowledge and minimal language barriers; global contractors offer cost savings and specialist skills, but risk hidden costs, language/culture barriers and difficulty controlling quality.

groups.title: Key influences — stakeholders
points: A stakeholder is an individual or group with a vested interest in, or affected by, a business's actions — not the same as a shareholder.
Employers hire and control employees, pay wages, and are responsible for a safe working environment and legal compliance; their goals include efficiency, profitability and staff wellbeing.

Employees perform tasks for reward under an employer's control; modern employees increasingly seek challenging work, involvement in decisions, and flexible working arrangements such as working from home.
Unions (e.g. the Australian Workers' Union, NSW Nurses and Midwives' Association) negotiate better wages and conditions, represent employees in disputes, and advise on legal rights.
Employer associations (e.g. the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry) represent and advise businesses, especially small ones, in collective bargaining and before industrial tribunals.

Government organisations act as employers, legislators (creating employment law), administrators/enforcers (e.g. the Fair Work Commission, Fair Work Ombudsman, Safe Work Australia) and economic managers (fiscal and monetary policy affecting employment).

The Fair Work Commission enforces the Fair Work Act 2009, sets the minimum wage, resolves disputes, and oversees three types of employment contracts: modern awards (minimum industry-wide terms), enterprise agreements (negotiated at the workplace level, approved via the Better Off Overall Test) and individual/common law contracts (negotiated one-to-one, usually for senior roles).
Society expects employers to comply with employment law, act ethically and socially responsibly (including toward outsourced/overseas workers), and uphold worker safety and equal opportunity.

groups.title: Key influences — legal, economic, technological, social and ethical
points: The employment contract is a legally binding agreement based on common law, setting out employer obligations (paying wages, safe environment, following the law) and employee obligations (performing tasks competently, following instructions, acting in good faith).

The National Employment Standards (NES) are 11 minimum entitlements all Australian employees receive regardless of contract type, covering matters like maximum weekly hours, leave entitlements and redundancy pay. The national minimum wage (from 1 July 2026) is $26.44 per hour ($1,004.90 for a 38-hour week), and no contract can pay below it.

Work Health and Safety (WHS) law (the Work Health and Safety Act 2011) requires employers to provide a safe system of work and requires all employers to hold workers' compensation insurance; benefits include fewer accidents and better productivity, while non-compliance risks fines, prosecution or business closure — industrial manslaughter offences now exist across most Australian jurisdictions, including NSW, carrying substantial fines and imprisonment for the most serious breaches.

Anti-discrimination and equal employment opportunity (EEO) law makes it illegal to discriminate on grounds like sex, age, disability or race — key legislation includes the Sex Discrimination Act 1984, the Age Discrimination Act 2004 and the Disability Discrimination Act 1992, all enforced through the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC); the Workplace Gender Equality Agency (WGEA) promotes gender equality specifically.

Economic influences: during a boom, demand for labour rises and the supply of available workers falls, giving employees more bargaining power and pushing wages up; during a downturn, demand for labour falls and businesses may reduce staff hours or numbers.

Technological influences: technology enables flexible/remote work (improving work-life balance), creates demand for new skills (requiring recruitment and retraining), and can cause redundancies when tasks are automated; AI in particular is forecast to add significant economic value but raises challenges around data quality, privacy, and the need for new technical skills.

Social influences — changing work patterns: demand for work-life balance and flexible/remote work (reinforced by the new right to disconnect, letting employees refuse unreasonable out-of-hours contact), rising job mobility increasing staff turnover, more women in the workforce (requiring equal pay and childcare flexibility), and an ageing workforce needing more flexible arrangements to encourage later retirement. Australia's high living standards can be undermined when HR functions are outsourced overseas without regard for those workers' conditions.

Ethics and corporate social responsibility in HR means providing positive working conditions, a safe environment, and fair treatment beyond the legal minimum — a positive workplace improves staff morale and reduces turnover, while an unethical one risks legal costs, industrial disputes and reputational damage. Intentional underpayment of wages (wage theft) became a criminal offence under Commonwealth law from 1 January 2025.

groups.title: Processes of human resource management
points: HR manages employees through four ongoing processes: acquisition, development, maintenance and separation — together forming the employment lifecycle from hiring to departure.

Acquisition moves from identifying a staffing need, through job analysis (defining the role's duties and required skills), to recruitment. Internal recruitment (promoting or transferring existing staff) is cheaper, faster and boosts morale by showing a career path, but limits fresh perspectives. External recruitment (advertising to the wider labour market) brings new skills and ideas, but is slower, more expensive and carries more onboarding risk. Selection (interviews, testing, reference checks) and a proper induction — including a legally required WHS induction — complete the process.

Development covers both training (building skills for an employee's current role, e.g. on-the-job coaching) and development proper (building skills for future or more senior roles, e.g. formal courses, secondments). It's an investment: it improves productivity, retention and succession planning, but is a cost the business must recover through improved performance.
Maintenance retains skilled staff through performance management, remuneration, and a safe, supportive workplace — reducing the direct and indirect cost of having to replace them.

Separation is voluntary (resignation, retirement) or involuntary (dismissal for underperformance/misconduct, or redundancy where a role is no longer needed). Whatever the type, a business must manage separations professionally and lawfully — proper notice, entitlements and, where possible, exit interviews — to limit legal risk and protect the morale of remaining staff. Telstra's 2024 restructuring, cutting around 2,800 roles (about 9% of its workforce) for roughly $350 million in targeted savings, was criticised on ethical rather than legal grounds since it came alongside continued profitability — a reminder that a lawful separation process can still raise questions about corporate social responsibility.

groups.title: Strategies in human resource management
points: Leadership style shapes HR effectiveness: autocratic leadership (directive, retains control) suits crises or highly regulated environments; democratic/participative leadership (involves staff in decisions) builds engagement and buy-in; laissez-faire leadership (minimal direction) suits highly skilled, autonomous teams. The right style depends on the workforce and situation, and feeds directly into corporate culture and turnover.

Job design: general job design (broad, varied tasks, via job enlargement or rotation) builds a flexible workforce but needs broader training; specific job design (narrow, specialised tasks) is efficient and quick to train for, but repetitive and less adaptable to change.

Recruitment strategy also considers skill scope: general-skills recruitment suits flexible or changing roles; specific-skills recruitment suits technical roles where deep expertise matters more than adaptability.

Training and development: training targets current-role skills (short-term, e.g. rolling out new software); development targets future capability (long-term, e.g. leadership programs) and feeds succession planning.

Performance management can be developmental (focused on improving future performance through feedback and coaching) or administrative (used to justify pay, promotion or termination decisions) — combining both in a single appraisal creates tension, since employees may be less candid about weaknesses if the same conversation determines their pay.

Rewards can be monetary (base pay, bonuses, profit share, performance pay) or non-monetary (flexible work, recognition, career development), and individual (rewards effort, but risks unhealthy competition) or group-based (rewards cooperation, but risks free-riding). Atlassian's flexible 'Team Anywhere' policy is a real example of a non-monetary reward outperforming pay on retention: 92% of employees say it lets them do their best work, and 91% cite it as an important reason for staying with the company.

Global HR strategy weighs cost (lower labour costs overseas), skills (accessing scarce or specialist skills unavailable domestically) and supply (labour availability across markets) against the ethical exposure of operating under weaker labour standards abroad.

groups.title: Workplace disputes
points: Workplace disputes arise from disagreements over pay, conditions, job security, workload or treatment — common causes include poor communication, unmet expectations, or change introduced without consultation.

Disputes carry both direct costs (lost production, legal costs, wages paid during stoppages) and indirect costs (reputational damage, reduced morale, harder recruitment) — and can extend beyond the business itself to suppliers, customers and the wider economy when disruption is significant.

Real example: from 21 November to 7 December 2024, around 1,500 workers at four Woolworths distribution centres in Victoria and NSW took protected industrial action over the 'Framework' electronic pick-rate system and pay. The 17-day dispute cost Woolworths an estimated $140 million in lost sales before it was resolved through negotiation, with pay rises and changes to how the system was applied.

Dispute resolution methods, in escalating order: negotiation (the parties resolve the issue directly, no third party, keeps the relationship intact); mediation (a neutral third party facilitates discussion but has no power to impose a decision); grievance procedures (a formal internal process, generally required under awards and agreements, giving employees a structured path to raise concerns); and courts and tribunals — the Fair Work Commission handles conciliation (non-binding facilitated discussion) and arbitration (a binding decision), with the most serious matters escalating to courts like the Federal Court.

Real example of court involvement: in 2020, Qantas outsourced its entire ground-handling operation, terminating around 1,820 employees. The Federal Court found this was partly done to prevent workers exercising their workplace rights, and in August 2025 imposed a $90 million penalty — the largest in Australian industrial relations history — on top of a separate $120 million compensation fund for affected workers.

groups.title: Effectiveness of human resource management
points: HR effectiveness is judged against a business's broader objectives — profitability, growth, efficiency and social responsibility — not just cost per employee, using indicators tracked over time and benchmarked against competitors or industry standards.

Corporate culture — the shared values, norms and behaviours of a workplace — is measured through staff surveys, external reviews and complaint/exit data. Real example: Rio Tinto's 2024 'Everyday Respect' Progress Review (over 11,600 contributions) found reported bullying rose from 31% (2021) to 39% (2024), while about half of respondents perceived improvement — showing a rising figure doesn't automatically mean HR is failing, since greater willingness to report can itself reflect a safer culture.

Benchmarking key variables compares HR metrics against internal targets, past performance, or competitors/industry standards. Real example: Wesfarmers publishes Total Recordable Injury Frequency Rate (TRIFR) by division; after Bunnings recorded the group's weakest safety result (17.0 in FY2024), it improved to 13.7 in FY2025 — evidence that publishing a disaggregated, benchmarked metric can itself drive corrective action.

Changes in staff turnover — the rate at which employees leave — raises recruitment and training costs when high and often signals dissatisfaction, though low turnover isn't automatically positive if it reflects a lack of outside opportunities rather than genuine engagement.
Absenteeism (unplanned staff absence) is an early warning sign of low morale, poor culture, stress or unsafe conditions, increasingly linked to employers' WHS duties to manage psychosocial hazards.

Accidents (injury frequency and severity, e.g. TRIFR/LTIFR) are both a legal obligation under work health and safety law and a direct cost through compensation claims, lost productivity and reputational damage.

Levels of disputation — working days lost to industrial action, grievances and matters before the Fair Work Commission or courts — a low level isn't proof of effective HR on its own, since it can also reflect employees who feel unable to raise concerns.

Worker satisfaction is measured through engagement surveys, flexibility uptake and retention data. Real example: Atlassian reports 92% of employees say its flexible 'Team Anywhere' policy lets them do their best work, and 91% cite it as an important reason for staying — directly linking a satisfaction indicator to the turnover indicator.

questions.questionHtml: How does an effective human resource function help a business achieve its long-term strategic goals? Explain your answer.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Link HR to productivity and profit maximisation.
  • Name at least two ways productivity is maximised.
Sample answer

The strategic role of HR is to assist the business in achieving its overall goal of profit maximisation, primarily through productivity — ensuring employees work to their fullest potential relative to the inputs used. When productivity is maximised, costs are minimised and profit is maximised.

Productivity is maximised through open communication and clear goal setting, so teams understand what they're working towards; eliminating conflict, since employees can't be productive while constantly in dispute; motivating staff by rewarding performance, which also reduces staff turnover; and creating a positive work environment where employees feel respected and valued. Businesses spend more than half their total costs on staff, so treating employees as an asset rather than just an expense, and maximising their productivity, can translate directly into a competitive advantage through lower costs and improved performance.

questions.questionHtml: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of outsourcing human resource functions to a domestic contractor versus a global contractor.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define outsourcing/contractors in HR.
  • Cover both domestic and global, with an advantage and disadvantage for each.
Sample answer

Outsourcing HR functions to a contractor gives a business access to specialised skills, potentially better quality, and lower costs than performing the function in-house. Domestic contractors offer expert knowledge of the local market and convenience, since they operate in the same time zone with minimal language barriers, though they may be more expensive than an equivalent overseas provider.

Global contractors can offer greater cost savings due to cheaper labour and favourable exchange rates, and can bring specialist skills and knowledge that improve productivity and flexibility, as well as transforming business culture through enhanced diversity. However, global contracting carries greater risk of hidden costs, language and cultural differences leading to lost-in-translation instructions, more difficulty controlling quality and reliability, and exposure to different (and potentially weaker) legal protections in the contractor's home country. A business needs to weigh cost savings against these added risks when choosing between domestic and global contractors.

questions.questionHtml: Explain ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of outsourcing human resource functions.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain one advantage.
  • Explain one disadvantage.
  • Apply each to a business context.
Sample answer

An advantage of outsourcing HR functions such as payroll or recruitment is access to specialist expertise and technology a business may not have in-house, while freeing internal staff to focus on strategic HR work rather than administrative processing — this is particularly valuable for a smaller business that cannot justify employing a full specialist HR team. A disadvantage is reduced control over a process central to the employment relationship: an outsourced provider may not understand the business's specific culture or urgent needs as well as internal staff would, and any errors — for example in payroll accuracy or in how a recruitment process reflects on the business's employer brand — can damage trust with employees or candidates even though the business itself did not directly cause the error.

questions.questionHtml: Outline the difference between a modern award, an enterprise agreement and an individual employment contract.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define all three types.
  • Note who they apply to and how they're approved.
Sample answer

A modern award sets the legally binding minimum terms and conditions for a specific industry, automatically applying to every employer and employee within it, covering matters like base pay, hours and superannuation — it's the most basic and widely used type of employment contract in Australia.

An enterprise agreement is negotiated at the level of an individual business between an employer (or group of employers) and a group of employees or their union, setting terms that must be above the National Employment Standards and approved by the Fair Work Commission using the Better Off Overall Test.

An individual (common law) contract is a personal agreement negotiated directly between an employer and one employee, usually used for senior roles like managers, offering less formal protection than the other two but still meeting the National Employment Standards as a legal minimum.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how economic conditions (a boom versus a downturn) influence human resource management decisions.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain the boom scenario and its HR effect.
  • Explain the downturn scenario and its HR effect.
Sample answer

During a boom, demand for labour rises as businesses need to produce more to meet growing customer demand, while the supply of available workers falls since more people already have jobs. This gives employees greater bargaining power, meaning businesses must offer higher wages and more benefits to attract and retain staff, and HR's focus shifts to recruitment.

During a downturn (bust), demand for labour falls as customers spend less and businesses produce less, while the supply of available workers rises as more people are looking for work. Employee bargaining power falls, and businesses may need to let staff go or reduce hours from full-time to casual or part-time, increasing costs like redundancy payments in the short term but reducing labour costs over the long run. HR's focus shifts to managing this separation process fairly and legally.

questions.questionHtml: Discuss how technological change, including AI, is influencing human resource management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Cover both benefits (flexibility, recruitment of new skills) and challenges (redundancies).
  • Reference AI specifically, with at least one concrete benefit and challenge.
Sample answer

Technology allows more flexible, remote work, which can improve employees' work-life balance and access to a wider pool of skilled workers globally. It also creates demand for new skills, meaning HR must recruit employees competent with modern technologies or retrain existing staff — for example, teaching factory workers to operate new machinery.

However, new technology like robotics can make some roles redundant, since tasks that used to require a person can now be done more efficiently by a machine, creating short-term redundancy costs and leaving some employees with non-transferable skills. Artificial intelligence is a major current example: it can automate repetitive tasks and improve decision-making using large datasets, and Australian businesses could generate significant additional economic value from AI over the next 15 years. However, it also raises challenges HR must manage, including the need for specialised technical skills that are in short supply, data privacy concerns, and the risk of biased or non-transparent AI systems if not implemented ethically. HR must balance capturing these benefits with managing the workforce and ethical risks they create.

questions.questionHtml: A logistics company's management team is negotiating a new enterprise agreement that would raise wages by 4% annually, but would also extend the required notice period for shift swaps and remove one paid tea break per shift. With reference to this scenario, explain why employees and employers might disagree about the proposal.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Identify the employer's interest in the proposal.
  • Identify the employee interest that conflicts with it.
  • Note how the conflict might be resolved.
Sample answer

The employer's interest in this proposed agreement is operational flexibility and cost control — a longer shift-swap notice period makes rostering more predictable for the business, and removing one paid tea break per shift directly reduces its labour costs. This conflicts with employees' interests in fair pay and reasonable working conditions: while a 4% wage rise is a genuine benefit, losing a paid break effectively increases the unpaid portion of every shift, and a longer notice period for shift swaps makes it harder for employees to respond to changes in their personal circumstances. This is a clear example of the tension between an employer's efficiency and cost objectives and employees' interest in their overall conditions, not just their headline pay rate — and it would typically be resolved through negotiation, potentially with union involvement, and ultimately must pass the Fair Work Commission's better off overall test before the agreement can be approved.

questions.questionHtml: A cleaning services company employs 900 staff, 76% of them on award rates. Wages make up 38% of its total costs. With reference to this business, explain the effect on it of a rise in the national minimum wage.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Note the current minimum wage figure.
  • Apply the effect to this business given its cost structure.
  • Note a possible business response.
Sample answer

As of 1 July 2026, the national minimum wage rose to $26.44 per hour ($1004.90 for a 38-hour week), with modern award rates increasing alongside it, which matters here because 76% of this business's 900 staff are paid on award rates. Because wages already make up 38% of the business's total costs, and the large majority of its workforce sits on rates directly tied to the award system, a minimum wage and award increase flows through to a very large share of its cost base at once — far more than it would for a business with a smaller proportion of award-reliant staff. This significantly increases the business's total labour cost and puts pressure on its profit margin unless it can pass some of the increase on through higher prices, and the business may also need to review its staffing levels and contract pricing to manage the higher cost per hour of labour.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the steps involved in the acquisition of new staff, and the trade-off between internal and external recruitment.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Sequence the acquisition steps.
  • Compare internal and external recruitment.
Sample answer

Acquisition begins with identifying a staffing need through workforce planning, followed by job analysis, which defines the role's duties and the skills required. From there, a business chooses between internal recruitment — promoting or transferring an existing employee — and external recruitment — advertising to the wider labour market.

Internal recruitment is cheaper and faster, since the candidate is already known to the business, and it boosts morale by showing staff a genuine career path. External recruitment is slower and more expensive, but brings fresh skills and perspectives the existing workforce may lack. Once a candidate is selected through interviews, testing and reference checks, a proper induction — including the legally required WHS induction — completes the acquisition process and helps the new employee become productive faster.

questions.questionHtml: Discuss how a business should manage an involuntary separation, such as a large-scale redundancy.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Distinguish voluntary from involuntary separation.
  • Cover legal obligations and the effect on remaining staff.
  • Reference a real example.
Sample answer

Separation is voluntary when an employee chooses to leave (resignation, retirement) or involuntary when the business ends the employment relationship (dismissal for underperformance, or redundancy where a role is no longer needed). Involuntary separation, especially on a large scale, carries the greatest legal and reputational risk.

A business managing a redundancy must provide proper notice and redundancy entitlements under the National Employment Standards, consult with affected staff where required, and consider support such as redeployment or outplacement assistance. Telstra's 2024 restructuring, cutting around 2,800 roles for roughly $350 million in targeted savings, was lawful and consultative in process, but still drew criticism because it came alongside continued profitability — a reminder that separation must be managed not just legally, but ethically, and with attention to the morale of the staff who remain after the process is complete.

questions.questionHtml: An insurance company is closing 25 regional offices and will make 210 staff redundant over four months. It has offered redeployment to 60 of them. With reference to this scenario, explain what the business should do to manage the separation process appropriately.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain the obligation to consult and give notice.
  • Explain the role of redundancy entitlements and support.
  • Note the risk of managing this poorly.
Sample answer

Managing an involuntary separation of this scale requires the insurer to consult with affected staff and their representatives before the redundancies are finalised, provide the notice periods and redundancy entitlements required under the National Employment Standards, and offer support such as outplacement services or, as it has already done, redeployment opportunities — here for 60 of the 210 affected staff. Handling this process well, with clear communication about timelines and genuine support for those affected, reduces the legal risk of an unfair dismissal claim and helps protect the company's reputation as an employer, including among the staff who remain employed after the restructure. If the process is managed poorly — for example, with inadequate consultation or unclear communication about who will and won't be redeployed — the business risks legal claims, damaged morale among remaining staff, and reputational harm that could affect its ability to recruit in the future.

questions.questionHtml: Distinguish between developmental and administrative approaches to performance management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define both purposes.
  • Note the tension when both are combined.
Sample answer

A developmental approach to performance management focuses on improving an employee's future performance through regular feedback, coaching and identifying training needs — its purpose is growth, not judgement.

An administrative approach uses performance management to inform decisions about pay, promotion or termination, treating the appraisal as a formal record used to justify a business outcome. Combining both purposes in a single appraisal process creates tension: an employee is less likely to be candid about their weaknesses if the same conversation will determine their next pay rise, which can undermine the honest feedback a developmental approach depends on.

questions.questionHtml: Discuss the effectiveness of flexible working arrangements as a non-monetary reward strategy, referring to a real business example.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain monetary vs non-monetary rewards.
  • Use a real, quantified example.
  • Reach a judgement.
Sample answer

Rewards can be monetary (base pay, bonuses, performance pay) or non-monetary (flexibility, recognition, career development). Flexible work is a non-monetary reward that costs a business relatively little to offer, since it changes how and where work happens rather than increasing wage costs directly.

Atlassian's 'Team Anywhere' policy, letting staff work from any location where the business has a legal entity, is real evidence this can be highly effective: 92% of employees say it lets them do their best work, and 91% cite it as an important reason for staying with the company — directly linking a non-monetary reward to the staff turnover indicator. This suggests flexibility can outperform financial reward on retention, particularly for skilled employees who have other job options and value autonomy over incremental pay increases. However, its effectiveness depends on the nature of the work — it suits roles that don't require physical presence, and a business with location-dependent operations (like retail or manufacturing) cannot offer the same reward.

questions.questionHtml: A real-estate agency pays its sales agents a low base salary plus commission of up to 50% of salary tied to individual property sales, while its administrative staff receive a fixed salary and share in an annual office-wide bonus pool. With reference to this scenario, discuss how effective performance-based pay is likely to be as a reward strategy.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Discuss the sales agents' individual performance pay.
  • Discuss the administrative team's group-based reward.
  • Reach a conclusion about when each is effective.
Sample answer

The sales agents' individual commission, worth up to 50% of salary, is likely to be an effective motivator specifically because an individual agent's property sales are clearly measurable and directly attributable to their own effort, giving a strong, fair incentive to perform — though it also risks encouraging short-term, self-interested behaviour, such as pressuring a client toward a quick sale that isn't in their long-term interest, if not carefully designed. The administrative team's fixed salary with an office-wide bonus pool reflects that individual administrative output is far harder to isolate and measure fairly than individual property sales, since much of that work is collaborative and supports the whole office — a group-based reward here avoids the unfairness and potential conflict of trying to rank individual contributions to shared support work, though it does mean an individual's reward is only loosely linked to their own personal effort. Overall, this shows performance-based pay is not a single strategy but needs to be matched to how measurable and individual the work actually is: it is more effective for the sales agents, where individual output is clear and directly revenue-generating, than it would be if applied in the same individual form to the more collaborative administrative roles.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the difference between negotiation and mediation as methods of resolving a workplace dispute.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define both methods.
  • Note the role of a third party and when each is used.
Sample answer

Negotiation is where the parties to a dispute resolve it directly between themselves, with no third party involved — it's the fastest and cheapest method, and keeps the ongoing working relationship intact, but only works if both sides are willing to compromise.

Mediation introduces a neutral third party who facilitates discussion between the parties, helping them reach their own agreement, but without the power to impose a binding outcome. It's typically used once direct negotiation has broken down, offering a more structured process while still preserving some control for both sides over the final result — unlike arbitration, where a third party (such as the Fair Work Commission) hands down a decision the parties must accept.

questions.questionHtml: Using a real example, discuss the costs to a business of a prolonged workplace dispute.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Cover direct and indirect costs.
  • Use a real, quantified example.
Sample answer

Workplace disputes carry direct costs — lost production, legal fees, and wages paid during stoppages — and indirect costs, including reputational damage, reduced morale among staff, and greater difficulty recruiting in future. These costs can also extend beyond the business itself, affecting suppliers and customers when disruption is significant.

The 2024 dispute at Woolworths' distribution centres illustrates this clearly: around 1,500 workers at four sites took 17 days of protected industrial action over an electronic pick-rate system and pay, which Woolworths estimated cost it $140 million in lost sales, alongside widely reported empty shelves in the lead-up to Christmas. The dispute was ultimately resolved through negotiation rather than arbitration, with pay rises and changes to how the system was applied — showing that the underlying cause (a system introduced without adequate consultation) was a far earlier, and cheaper, problem to have addressed than the dispute it went on to cause.

questions.questionHtml: Distinguish between negotiation and mediation as methods of resolving workplace disputes.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define negotiation.
  • Define mediation.
  • Note when each is appropriate.
Sample answer

Negotiation is a direct discussion between the employer and employee (or their representatives) to reach a mutually acceptable resolution, without any third party involved — it is generally the fastest and least costly method, and tends to preserve the working relationship best, but it depends on both sides being willing and able to compromise. Mediation involves an independent third party who facilitates discussion between the two sides but does not make a binding decision for them — this is appropriate when direct negotiation has broken down or when the relationship between the parties has become difficult enough that a neutral facilitator is needed to help them communicate productively, while still leaving the final resolution in the hands of the employer and employee themselves rather than being imposed by an external decision-maker.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how a business could use staff turnover and absenteeism together to assess the effectiveness of its human resource management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define both indicators.
  • Explain what a rise in each signals.
  • Note why using them together is more useful than either alone.
Sample answer

Staff turnover measures the rate at which employees leave a business, while absenteeism measures unplanned staff absence. A rise in either can signal underlying dissatisfaction, poor culture, or workload and management problems — but each captures a different stage of disengagement.

Absenteeism is typically a leading indicator: employees who are unhappy but not yet ready to resign often show it first through unplanned absence. Rising turnover is a lagging indicator, confirming that dissatisfaction has reached the point employees are actually leaving, which is more costly since it also creates recruitment and retraining expenses. Tracking both together lets a business identify a developing problem through absenteeism data before it shows up as a costly rise in turnover, giving HR an earlier opportunity to intervene.

questions.questionHtml: Evaluate the effectiveness of human resource management for a real Australian business, using at least two indicators.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name the business and be specific about what happened.
  • Use at least two named indicators with real, dated figures.
  • Reach a substantiated overall judgement.
Sample answer

Qantas's 2020 decision to outsource its entire ground-handling operation, terminating around 1,820 employees, is a clear case of ineffective HR management when judged against the levels of disputation and worker satisfaction indicators. The Federal Court found the decision was made partly to prevent employees exercising their workplace rights, including protected industrial action, and in August 2025 the Court imposed a $90 million penalty — the largest in Australian industrial relations history — on top of a separate $120 million compensation fund for affected workers.

Judged purely on short-term cost, outsourcing may have looked like an effective strategy, since it reduced the wage bill during a period of financial pressure for the airline. However, judged against the disputation indicator, the years of litigation and the record penalty show the strategy failed badly, and the reputational cost — including a public apology from the CEO and a judge describing the response as the 'wrong kind of sorry' — likely damaged worker satisfaction and public trust in the business as an employer well beyond the $210 million in direct penalties and compensation. This shows HR effectiveness has to be judged over the long term and against legal and ethical outcomes, not just an initial cost saving.

questions.questionHtml: A fast-food franchise's annual staff turnover has climbed from 22% to 39%, with exit interviews most often citing unpredictable shift scheduling and a lack of pay progression. With reference to this scenario, explain what the rising turnover figure indicates about the business's human resource management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State what the rise in turnover suggests.
  • Link it to the specific reasons given in the exit interviews.
  • Note the cost this creates for the business.
Sample answer

A rise in staff turnover from 22% to 39% is a strong indicator that the business's human resource management has weakened, since turnover reflects how well a business is retaining its employees and, indirectly, how satisfied they are. The specific reasons cited in exit interviews point to identifiable HR failures rather than an unavoidable external cause: unpredictable shift scheduling suggests weaknesses in the business's maintenance strategies around work-life balance, and a lack of pay progression suggests its reward and development strategies are not giving staff a visible path to earn more over time. This rise is costly for the business well beyond the immediate loss of experienced staff — it also means bearing the recruitment and induction costs of replacing close to two in five of its workforce each year, and the loss of accumulated product and customer knowledge that harms customer service in the meantime.

questions.questionHtml: Horizon Homewares employs 1200 staff across 40 stores. Over the past twelve months, staff turnover climbed from 15% to 28%, absenteeism increased from 2.4 to 4.9 days per employee, and satisfaction with training and career opportunities on its internal staff survey dropped from 68% to 41%. Sales per employee also fell 9% over the same period. With reference to this scenario, judge how effective Horizon Homewares' human resource management has been, and recommend TWO alternative strategies it could adopt.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Evaluate what the indicators together show.
  • Recommend a strategy addressing career development.
  • Recommend a strategy addressing rostering or working conditions, and justify both.
Sample answer

Horizon Homewares' human resource management has clearly become significantly less effective over the past year, and the indicators reinforce rather than contradict one another: rising turnover (15% to 28%) and rising absenteeism (2.4 to 4.9 days) both signal falling staff morale, and the staff survey confirms the likely underlying cause, with satisfaction in training and career opportunities collapsing from 68% to 41%. The 9% fall in sales per employee shows this isn't just an HR-department problem — declining engagement is now measurably affecting business performance, plausibly through a mix of lost experienced staff, more days with fewer people rostered on, and lower motivation among those who remain. To address this, Horizon Homewares should first invest in a genuine career development and internal promotion pathway — given training and career opportunity satisfaction has fallen furthest and this is the most direct driver of the turnover exit interviews would likely confirm — for example structured training plans and clearer internal advancement criteria, which should improve retention and, over time, satisfaction and sales performance as more experienced staff remain. Second, given rising absenteeism often reflects burnout or scheduling problems, the business should review its rostering and staffing levels to ensure stores are adequately staffed, reducing the pressure on remaining staff that drives further absenteeism and turnover. The main limitation is that both strategies require upfront investment in training programs and additional staffing at a time when sales per employee has already fallen, so Horizon Homewares will need to accept short-term cost increases in order to reverse a trend that, left unaddressed, is likely to continue eroding both morale and sales performance.

trivia.questionHtml: What are HR's four main functions?
trivia.answerHtml: Acquisition, development, maintenance and separation.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the strategic role of HR?
trivia.answerHtml: To help the business achieve profit maximisation, mainly through maximising employee productivity.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between outsourcing and using a contractor?
trivia.answerHtml: Outsourcing gives an ongoing function to another business long-term; a contractor works on a specific project, then moves on.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a stakeholder?
trivia.answerHtml: An individual or group with a vested interest in, or affected by, a business's actions — not the same as a shareholder.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a trade union?
trivia.answerHtml: An organisation of workers that negotiates for better wages and conditions and represents employees in disputes.

trivia.questionHtml: What is an employer association?
trivia.answerHtml: An organisation that represents and assists businesses/employers, especially small businesses, e.g. the ACCI.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the Fair Work Commission?
trivia.answerHtml: Australia's industrial relations tribunal, created by the Fair Work Act 2009, which sets the minimum wage and resolves disputes.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a modern award?
trivia.answerHtml: Legally binding minimum terms and conditions of employment that apply automatically to a whole industry.

trivia.questionHtml: What is an enterprise agreement?
trivia.answerHtml: A negotiated agreement about pay and conditions at a specific workplace, approved by the Fair Work Commission.

trivia.questionHtml: What are the National Employment Standards (NES)?
trivia.answerHtml: 11 minimum employment entitlements that apply to all Australian employees regardless of contract type.

trivia.questionHtml: What is Australia's national minimum wage from 1 July 2026?
trivia.answerHtml: $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 for a 38-hour week.

trivia.questionHtml: What does the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 require of employers?
trivia.answerHtml: To provide a safe system of work and hold workers' compensation insurance.

trivia.questionHtml: Name one Commonwealth anti-discrimination law and what it covers.
trivia.answerHtml: The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 — prohibits discrimination based on sex, gender identity, marital status or pregnancy.

trivia.questionHtml: What does EEO stand for?
trivia.answerHtml: Equal Employment Opportunity — equitable policies and practices in recruitment, selection, training and promotion.

trivia.questionHtml: What does WGEA stand for and what does it do?
trivia.answerHtml: Workplace Gender Equality Agency — promotes and reviews compliance with gender equality in the workplace.

trivia.questionHtml: How does a boom in the economy affect the labour market?
trivia.answerHtml: Demand for labour rises and supply of available workers falls, giving employees more bargaining power.

trivia.questionHtml: How does an economic downturn affect HR's focus?
trivia.answerHtml: Demand for labour falls, so HR's focus shifts to managing the separation process (redundancies, reduced hours).

trivia.questionHtml: What social trend is increasing demand for flexible and remote work arrangements?
trivia.answerHtml: Changing work patterns — demand for work-life balance, more women in the workforce, and an ageing workforce.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a key challenge of adopting AI in HR/business, according to the notes?
trivia.answerHtml: It requires specialised technical skills that are in short supply, and raises data privacy and bias concerns.

trivia.questionHtml: What does the Fair Work Ombudsman do?
trivia.answerHtml: An independent statutory agency providing free advice on workplace rights and responsibilities to workers and employers.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the Better Off Overall Test (BOOT)?
trivia.answerHtml: The test the Fair Work Commission uses to approve an enterprise agreement, ensuring employees are better off than under the relevant award.

trivia.questionHtml: Give one example of corporate social responsibility in HR.
trivia.answerHtml: Providing positive, safe working conditions and fair treatment that go beyond the legal minimum.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the 'right to disconnect'?
trivia.answerHtml: An employee's right to refuse unreasonable employer contact outside working hours, phased in for larger and then smaller employers from 2024–2025.

trivia.questionHtml: What are the four processes of human resource management?
trivia.answerHtml: Acquisition, development, maintenance and separation.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the main advantage of internal recruitment over external recruitment?
trivia.answerHtml: It's cheaper and faster, and boosts morale by showing existing staff a career path.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between training and development?
trivia.answerHtml: Training builds skills for an employee's current role (short-term); development builds skills for future/more senior roles (long-term).

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between voluntary and involuntary separation?
trivia.answerHtml: Voluntary separation is the employee's choice (resignation, retirement); involuntary is the business's decision (dismissal or redundancy).

trivia.questionHtml: Name one leadership style relevant to HR strategy.
trivia.answerHtml: Autocratic, democratic/participative, or laissez-faire.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between general and specific job design?
trivia.answerHtml: General job design covers broad, varied tasks (flexible but needs broader training); specific job design covers narrow, specialised tasks (efficient but repetitive).

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between a developmental and an administrative approach to performance management?
trivia.answerHtml: Developmental focuses on improving future performance through feedback; administrative uses appraisal to justify pay, promotion or termination decisions.

trivia.questionHtml: Give an example of a non-monetary reward.
trivia.answerHtml: Flexible working arrangements, recognition, or career development opportunities.

trivia.questionHtml: What's a risk of group/team-based rewards?
trivia.answerHtml: Free-riding — some team members contribute less while still sharing the reward.

trivia.questionHtml: What three factors shape a business's global HR strategy?
trivia.answerHtml: Cost, skills and supply of labour in different markets.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the difference between negotiation and mediation in resolving a workplace dispute?
trivia.answerHtml: Negotiation is direct between the parties with no third party; mediation involves a neutral third party who facilitates but can't impose a decision.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between conciliation and arbitration at the Fair Work Commission?
trivia.answerHtml: Conciliation is non-binding facilitated discussion; arbitration is a binding decision handed down by the Commission.

trivia.questionHtml: What penalty did the Federal Court impose on Qantas in August 2025, and for what?
trivia.answerHtml: A $90 million penalty for unlawfully outsourcing its ground-handling workforce to prevent employees exercising workplace rights.

trivia.questionHtml: What caused the 2024 Woolworths distribution centre dispute?
trivia.answerHtml: The 'Framework' electronic pick-rate system and pay — resolved after 17 days of industrial action, costing an estimated $140 million in lost sales.

trivia.questionHtml: Name the seven indicators of HR effectiveness in the syllabus.
trivia.answerHtml: Corporate culture, benchmarking key variables, changes in staff turnover, absenteeism, accidents, levels of disputation, and worker satisfaction.

trivia.questionHtml: What did Rio Tinto's 2024 'Everyday Respect' review find about reported bullying?
trivia.answerHtml: It rose from 31% in 2021 to 39% in 2024 — though the company attributes part of this to greater willingness to report.

trivia.questionHtml: What is TRIFR, and which company benchmarks it publicly by division?
trivia.answerHtml: Total Recordable Injury Frequency Rate — Wesfarmers publishes it for Bunnings, Kmart, Officeworks and other divisions.
